passages.happening:
Jehoram son of Ahab becomes king of Israel in Samaria and reigns twelve years. He does evil, ‘but not as his father and mother had done’ (verse 2). He removes the sacred pillar of Baal his father made, but he clings to the sins of Jeroboam (verses 2-3).

Mesha king of Moab, a sheep breeder, had paid Israel a yearly tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. After Ahab's death he rebels (verses 4-5). Jehoram asks Jehoshaphat of Judah to march with him, and Jehoshaphat answers, “I will go,” and, “I am like you, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses” (verse 7). They go by the Desert of Edom, with the king of Edom.

After seven days on a roundabout route they have no water for the army or the animals (verse 9). The king of Israel says that the LORD has called three kings out only to hand them to Moab (verse 10). Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him” (verse 11). A servant names Elisha, who ‘used to pour water on the hands of Elijah’ (verse 11). Jehoshaphat says, “The word of the LORD is with him” (verse 12), and the three kings go down to him.
passages.hearers:
The rebellion mentioned in passing in 1:1 now comes to a head. Jehoram, also spelled Joram, reigned about 852 to 841 BC. He is less devoted to Baal than his parents, but he keeps Jeroboam's calves.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a plateau of pasture suited to sheep, and its tribute of lambs and wool fits its economy. It had been subject to Israel since Omri. The Mesha Stele, a black basalt inscription found at Dhiban, the Bible's Dibon, in 1868, is Mesha's own record. In it he says that Omri oppressed Moab because the Moabite god Chemosh was angry with his land, that Omri's son carried it on, and that Mesha threw off Israel's control and took Israelite towns. The stele does not describe this campaign, and the two accounts are hard to fit together in detail, but they agree on the main fact: under Mesha, Moab broke free.

The allies go round the south end of the Dead Sea through Edom, which was then subject to Judah, so its king here was probably a dependent ruler. Jehoshaphat's words repeat almost exactly what he said to Ahab before Ramoth-gilead, and once again he asks for a prophet of the LORD. To pour water on someone's hands was the work of a personal servant or disciple.
passages.later: Jehoshaphat had said the same words to Ahab before Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22:4), and that alliance ended in Ahab's death. Moab was also Ruth's country. A Moabite woman once made a pledge that went further than any treaty: ‘your people will be my people, and your God will be my God’ (Ruth 1:16).
passages.asks: The kings went seven days on their own plan before anyone asked for the LORD's word. Ask how far you go on your own plans before you pray about them. And ask whom you would go to, as Jehoshaphat did, when you need to hear the truth.

passages.t: Water from nowhere, and a land laid waste
passages.happening:
Elisha says to the king of Israel, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” (verse 13). He would not even look at him, he says, but for his regard for Jehoshaphat (verse 14). He asks for a harpist, and as the harpist plays, ‘the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha’ (verse 15).

The LORD's word is to dig the valley full of ditches. ‘You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water’ (verse 17). The LORD will also give Moab into their hand, and they are to attack every fortified city, cut down every good tree, stop up every spring and ruin every good field with stones (verses 18-19). The next morning, ‘at the time of the morning sacrifice, water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land’ (verse 20).

The Moabites, gathered at the border, see the sun shining red on the water. “This is blood!” they cry. “The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” (verse 23). They rush into Israel's camp and are routed. The allies destroy the cities, cover the good fields with stones, stop the springs and cut down the trees, until only Kir-haraseth is left standing, under attack from slingers (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Elisha shows the same blunt independence as Elijah. He helps the king of Israel only for Jehoshaphat's sake. Music went with prophecy in Israel, and the verb for the harpist's playing is the one used of David playing the lyre before Saul. The music is a setting for receiving God's word, not a way of producing it.

The sudden water fits a known feature of the region. Rain in the highlands of Edom can send flash floods down dry valleys far from where any rain falls. God gives water in the desert by means the soldiers never see, ‘at the time of the morning sacrifice’ (verse 20).

Water ties the chapter together. The armies have none, it comes without wind or rain, and the same water, red in the morning sun, deceives the Moabites.

Destroying trees, springs and fields crippled an enemy's economy for years. It stands in tension with the law's rule against cutting down fruit trees in a siege, and interpreters differ on whether Elisha's word in verse 19 is a command or a prediction of what would happen. Kir-haraseth, Moab's stronghold, is usually identified with Kerak in Jordan, a naturally fortified hilltop.
passages.later: The law said of a siege, ‘you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit’ (Deuteronomy 20:19).
passages.asks: Elisha said the water would come without wind or rain. Ask when help has come to you by a road you did not see. And ask what it would mean to be faithful enough, like Jehoshaphat, that others are helped for your sake.

passages.happening: When the king of Moab sees that the battle is too fierce for him, he takes seven hundred swordsmen and tries to break through to the king of Edom, but they fail (verse 26). ‘So he took his firstborn son, who was to succeed him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the city wall’ (verse 27). ‘And there was great fury against the Israelites, so they withdrew and returned to their own land’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Child sacrifice was practiced in parts of the ancient world, especially in times of crisis, and Israel's law forbade it absolutely. Mesha offered his heir on the wall in sight of the besiegers, presumably to Chemosh, in a desperate appeal to his god. The Mesha Stele shows how Moab read its history by Chemosh's anger and favor, much as Israel read its history by the LORD's.

The word for burnt offering, olah, is the word for Israel's daily offerings to the LORD, and its use here is shocking by design. It also recalls Abraham on the mountain, where God provided a ram in place of the son.

The ending is abrupt. After verse upon verse of fulfillment, the last verse reverses the outcome, and the narrator does not explain it.
passages.later: The law said, ‘They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods’ (Deuteronomy 12:31), and forbade Israel to worship that way. Micah asked, ‘Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression’ (Micah 6:7), and answered, “And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
Why did Israel withdraw after Mesha sacrificed his son, and whose fury fell on them?

The text says only that there was great fury against Israel, and interpreters have long disagreed about what that means. The word, qetseph, most often means the LORD's wrath, so one view is that God's anger fell on Israel, perhaps for the excess of the campaign, the ruin of trees and fields, or something that made Israel share in the horror, though the text does not say what. A second view is that the fury was human: Israel's own revulsion at the sight, or Moab's rage and renewed resistance, or Edom's anger, since Mesha had tried to break through to the king of Edom, and the alliance broke. A third view, held by some critical scholars, is that the story keeps the Moabite belief that Chemosh's anger drove Israel back, without the narrator granting that Chemosh was real.

What the chapter does not do is suggest that the sacrifice worked as Mesha hoped. The rest of Scripture condemns it as an abomination. The text names the act in one verse and does not describe it, and these notes do the same. The narrator leaves the ending unexplained, and an honest reading admits the uncertainty.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Mesha gave up his son in the hope of saving his city. Ask what people give up today, even the good of their own children, to the things they hope will save them. And ask what it means that the God of Israel asks for justice, mercy and a humble walk, not a child.
